properties.name: A write cannot silently lose someone else's work, and a baseline cannot be established from a digest nobody read
properties.statement:
On a shared graph, a write must be able to say what it is about to overwrite, and refuse when the caller's assumption about the current value is stale. (Distinct from the triage FACT the guard named: that records what was reported and when; this is what must become true.)

THE MEASURED CASE, OBSERVED FROM BOTH SIDES OF ONE COLLISION, which is what makes it structural rather than unlucky. A worker read `frag:ownership_guard`; ninety seconds later another attached session wrote it; the write returned a normal success with the full node body and nothing unusual. THE WINNER WAS NEVER TOLD. The loser found out only because `record_change` happens to RETURN the snapshot it took — a diagnostic side-effect of an unrelated tool, not a guard. Had they used any other write path, both would have believed they made the change and one would have been wrong.

⇒ `create_node` has NO expected-current-value parameter, so no write can be made conditional on what was read, and `claim_region` is advisory with nothing consulting it before a write. On a shared graph with several attached sessions, every property edit is a lost update waiting to happen and detection is left to luck.

PARTLY MITIGATED SINCE, and it is detection rather than prevention: `create_node` now returns a `revision` block naming the properties it replaced, their prior values, and a `prior_content_hash`. That hash is exactly the raw material a compare-and-swap needs; nothing consumes it yet.

THREE RELATED FAILURES OF THE SAME SHAPE — a write that destroys without saying so:

(a) RE-USING AN EXISTING NODE ID IN AN INGEST PASS IS A WRITE, NOT A REFERENCE, and there is no cite-only form. A worker silently reverted a USER-RULED restoration with their next batch — on the one node their fleet was already watching, which that same worker had personally restored thirty minutes earlier and written the report explaining why it mattered.

(b) `set_artifact_checksum` ACCEPTS A MALFORMED DIGEST WITHOUT COMPLAINT. A 13-character value was stored and echoed back as correct, with a `change_event_id` and a `baseline_established` disposition. A truncated baseline can never match a real digest, so it reports `checksum_change` forever against a file that never changed — a permanent false drift alarm seeded by the act meant to establish truth.

(c) THERE IS NO DISPOSITION MEANING "THE BASELINE I RECORDED WAS WRONG". `set_artifact_checksum` is correctly one-shot, so the only route back is `create_node` merging the field directly — which bypasses the ChangeEvent the one-shot design exists to force. The safe correction path leaves no record; the recorded path asserts something false about the content having moved.

⚠️ AND THE HARDER HALF, which the reporter states plainly and which I can corroborate from the other direction: their second bad checksum was WELL-FORMED at 64 characters and simply WRONG — "typed from memory rather than read from `sha256sum`". No shape guard catches that. I made the identical error on 2026-08-16, retyping a digest I had displayed truncated, into `art:schema-build` — the drift baseline whose whole job is noticing when design and build disagree. A shape guard would have caught their first case and neither of ours. Whether anything can catch the second is the open part.

REPORTED BY dev_storyflow's fleet, 2026-08-09 and 2026-08-15, corroborated across seats.
